\chapter{Green and Yellow}
\label{ch:fr-green-and-yellow}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name green and yellow in French, and say how solid the claimed link between jaune and German gelb actually is.}

Say vert as the ordinary Romance inheritance from viridis, say jaune as galbinus 'yellow-green', and state the jaune / gelb cousinhood as probable rather than certain. The chapter's only lesson, so the payoff covers everything it introduces.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vert, jaune]{vert, jaune — the expected inheritance, and a hidden PIE-level cousin}

\label{lesson:FR-C23-vert-jaune}



\begin{quote}
French's green word is exactly what you'd expect. Its yellow word hides something you won't expect at all — a secret cousin sitting inside German.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vert} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{viridis} — and this is genuinely the \textbf{standard} source of \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{} across nearly every Romance language: Spanish \emph{verde}, Italian \emph{verde}, Portuguese \emph{verde}, Catalan \emph{verd}. No surprise here — a clean, shared inheritance.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jaune} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yellow}\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{galbinus}, which literally meant \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yellow-green}\textquotedblright{} — an extended form of \textbf{galbus}, from \textbf{Proto-Indo- European} \emph{\textbf{*ghel-}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to shine}\textquotedblright{} (with derivatives covering green, yellow, and gold alike — the same root gives Greek \emph{khlōros}, \textquotedblleft{}greenish- yellow\textquotedblright{}). Here's the genuinely surprising part: this \textbf{same PIE root}, \emph{\textbf{*ghel-}}, is also usually cited as the source of \textbf{German}'s \textbf{gelb} and English's \textbf{yellow} — by a completely separate, Germanic path (Proto- Germanic \emph{\textbf{*gelwaz}}). Honesty check, though: the \emph{galbus}$\to$\emph{*ghel-} link itself is \textbf{less secure} than it looks — some modern Latin scholarship treats \emph{galbus}'s origin as unknown rather than confirming the connection. So \emph{jaune} and \emph{gelb} are \textbf{probably} cousins at the Proto-Indo-European level, despite one reaching French through Latin and the other reaching German directly through Germanic — just don't treat that link as airtight.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vert\textquotedblright{} — green, the standard Romance word
  \item \textquotedblleft{}jaune\textquotedblright{} — yellow, literally \textquotedblleft{}yellow-green\textquotedblright{}
  \item the probable cousin — \textquotedblleft{}jaune, gelb\textquotedblright{} — likely the same ancient PIE root, two completely different paths, though the link isn't airtight
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{vert} a typical or unusual Romance word for \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Typical} — the standard source across nearly all Romance languages.) What did Latin \textbf{galbinus}, the source of \emph{jaune}, literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Yellow-green}.\textquotedblright{}) What German word is usually called \emph{jaune}'s deep PIE cousin, and how solid is that link? (\textbf{Gelb} — both usually traced to PIE \emph{*ghel-}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine,\textquotedblright{} though modern Latin scholarship treats \emph{galbus}'s origin as genuinely unknown, so the connection is probable, not certain.)
\end{tcolorbox}
